response.summary:
The pipeline is well‑architected for its n=1 longitudinal context, with careful attention to time‑respecting backtesting, multiple‑comparison correction, and mediator exclusion. The walk‑forward XGBoost backtest uses an appropriate gap to avoid leakage from long‑lag features, and prediction intervals are calibrated from out‑of‑fold residuals. The causal layer employs doubly‑robust AIPW with time‑ordered cross‑fitting and block‑bootstrap CIs to account for autocorrelation. BH‑FDR is consistently applied across journal/habit/supplement/nutrition descriptive tests and across the joint causal family. The confounder set correctly excludes same‑night sleep/HRV mediators, focusing on pre‑treatment variables.

Two notable issues remain: (1) the SARIMAX exogenous feature preparation uses `bfill()` after `ffill()`, which can propagate future information backward into the training set, artificially improving walk‑forward performance; (2) the prediction intervals’ underlying residual standard deviation is assumed constant across the entire training period, though its stability is monitored via logged CI coverage. Multicollinearity is addressed by VIF‑based pruning in the Stage‑3 OLS and a computed condition‑number warning for SHAP, but no formal action is taken beyond warnings. The block‑bootstrap for AIPW relies on a fixed 7‑day block length without checking the actual autocorrelation structure of the influence values. These are mostly P1 or P2 concerns; the most impactful fix is removing bfill from SARIMAX exogenous preparation.

findings.title: SARIMAX exogenous features leak future information via bfill
findings.description: Before shifting and feeding to SARIMAX, exogenous features are prepared with `.ffill().bfill().asfreq('D')`. The backward fill pulls future observed values into the past, giving the model access to information not yet available at training time, artificially inflating walk‑forward forecast accuracy.
findings.evidence: Line 2333: `original_exog = (hrv_valid[exog_feats].copy().ffill().bfill().asfreq("D")`; the `.bfill()` propagates values backwards across any time gaps.
findings.recommendation: Remove `.bfill()`; use only forward fill (with a limit) or drop rows with missing exogenous values to maintain temporal integrity.

findings.title: SARIMAX shifted exogenous features also suffer from bfill leakage
findings.description: After shifting the exogenous matrix by one row (to align `exog[N]` with `original_exog[N-1]`), the pipeline again applies `.ffill().bfill()`. This backward fill can replace missing past values with future ones, leaking information.
findings.evidence: Line 2335: `exog = original_exog.shift(1).ffill().bfill()`; the `.bfill()` on the shifted series fills backward from the future into earlier rows.
findings.recommendation: Strip `.bfill()` from the shifted exogenous preparation; use forward fill only or ensure no gaps exist before shifting.

findings.title: Prediction interval standard deviation assumes stationarity of residuals
findings.description: The OOF residual standard deviation used for XGBoost prediction intervals is computed once across all training splits and reused for the entire evaluation period. While the logged CI coverage can detect drift, the intervals may be under‑ or over‑dispersed if residual variance changes systematically over time (e.g., due to new data sources or seasonal effects).
findings.evidence: `pred_std_by_horizon[h] = float(np.std(oof_resid))` computed once per horizon from the full dataset, then applied uniformly to all backtest and live predictions.
findings.recommendation: Consider recomputing the OOF standard deviation on a rolling basis (e.g., every 30 days) to adapt to possible non‑stationarity in model residuals.

findings.title: Fixed block‑bootstrap length may not match psi autocorrelation structure
findings.description: The block‑bootstrap for AIPW confidence intervals uses a hard‑coded block length of 7 days. If the influence values have different autocorrelation decay (e.g., shorter for some treatments), the bootstrap can over‑cover and reduce power unnecessarily.
findings.evidence: `AIPW_BOOTSTRAP_BLOCK_LEN = 7` used in `_block_bootstrap_ci` without empirical validation against the actual psi series.
findings.recommendation: Optionally, estimate the optimal block length from the data (e.g., using the method of Politis & White, 2004) or at least log a comparison with a default-length CI to flag mismatches.

findings.title: XGBoost multi‑horizon backtest reuses h=1 hyperparameters without horizon‑specific tuning
findings.description: The walk‑forward backtest for horizons h=2..7 reuses the XGBoost hyperparameters optimised for h=1. While efficient, the increasing prediction horizon may change the optimal bias‑variance trade‑off; performance degradation beyond h=1 might partly stem from mis‑tuning rather than genuine forecast difficulty.
findings.evidence: Line 2480: the `XGBRegressor` instantiation inside the `for h in HORIZONS` loop always uses `max_depth=4, learning_rate=0.05, n_estimators=200` with no per‑horizon Optuna or hyperparameter adaptation.
findings.recommendation: At minimum, document this choice as a deliberate trade‑off. If horizon‑specific MAE deteriorates more sharply than expected, consider a brief per‑horizon hyperparameter search (e.g., 10 trials) during retrain cycles.

things_done_well.title: Walk‑forward backtest with GAP_DAYS prevents feature‑window leakage
things_done_well.why_it_matters: The custom 28‑day embargo gap ensures that 28‑day rolling features (hrv_28d_mean, personal z‑scores) do not incorporate data from the test fold; this is essential for honest out‑of‑sample evaluation.

things_done_well.title: Mediator‑exclusion confounder set correctly isolates total effects
things_done_well.why_it_matters: The explicit exclusion of same‑night sleep/HRV variables from the confounder set avoids mediator‑adjustment bias, ensuring the reported ATE captures the full actionable effect of behavioural interventions.

things_done_well.title: AIPW cross‑fitting uses TimeSeriesSplit to respect temporal order
things_done_well.why_it_matters: Switching from randomised folds to `TimeSeriesSplit` prevents the outcome model from seeing near‑future HRV via autocorrelation, keeping cross‑fitting honest in a time‑series setting.

things_done_well.title: BH‑FDR is applied uniformly across descriptive and causal test families
things_done_well.why_it_matters: The pipeline corrects for multiple testing in every family (journal, habit, supplement, nutrition, global correlations, and the joint causal treatment family), preventing an estimated ~8–10 false positives per run.

questions_for_followup: What is the empirical coverage of the 80% prediction intervals in live operation, and does it remain stable across seasons? Access to the historical `ci_coverage` logs would clarify whether the assumption of constant residual variance is justified.

Are any of the continuous features (besides HRV) non‑stationary or trended over the 568‑day sample? An ADF test on training‑load and stress features would reveal whether their use in regression or as SARIMAX exogenous variables requires differencing.

How sensitive are the AIPW point estimates and E‑values to the confounder forward‑fill limit (currently 2 days)? Could a per‑treatment comparison with a stricter limit (1 day) or no ffill confirm the robustness of the current approach?
